zone: Cutthroat Pass, Methow Pass and the PCT north of Rainy Pass
_areas_note: ONE PEAK REMOVED. Whine Spire does not belong here — it is a tower on Silver Star Mountain's north ridge, attached to the Wine Spires, and it is reached by the Burgundy Col approach from the Silver Star Creek side of SR 20 far to the east. It shares no trailhead, no drainage and no camp with anything in this file, and its own zone already exists. The remaining four are all genuinely served by the Rainy Pass trailheads. Golden Horn and Tower Mountain are the Snowy Lakes pair, climbed from a camp reached by walking the Pacific Crest Trail north over Cutthroat, Granite and Methow Passes. Mount Hardy has two ways on: the same PCT line, leaving it near Methow Pass, or a much shorter roadside start from a highway pullout a couple of miles west of Rainy Pass, which is how most parties actually do it. Whistler Mountain is the odd one — it is a day scramble that begins in the Rainy Pass parking lot itself and never touches the backcountry camps below, so it is kept here for the trailhead it shares and nothing more. NOTHING HERE DUPLICATES THE CUTTHROAT PEAK FILE: that one covers the Cutthroat Creek trailhead, the lake basin, the south-side climbers' bivy and the developed campgrounds down-valley at Lone Fir, Klipchuck and Early Winters. This file covers the PCT crest north of Rainy Pass, which is a different trailhead reaching different ground, and the campgrounds are deliberately not repeated. This whole corridor is Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, NOT national park — there is no backcountry permit system anywhere in this file.

sites.name: Rainy Pass PCT north trailhead
sites.capacity: A large paved lot on the north-east side of the highway at the pass, shared between climbers, larch-season day hikers and long-distance walkers. It fills early on weekends from late summer onward and there is no overflow.
sites.water: None at the lot, and this matters more here than it looks. The crest north of the pass is dry, so what you carry out of the car is what you have until well down the far side.
sites.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. No camping permit, no quota and nothing to reserve anywhere in this zone — this is national forest, and the park permit system that governs the country west of here does not apply.
sites.notes: Everything in this file starts from this lot. It is also the start of Whistler Mountain, which is unlike the rest: head east from the parking area into the second gully and follow it to the summit, about four miles round trip and three thousand feet of gain, and no camp in this file helps in the slightest. There is a toilet and no water. Parties routinely sleep in the car here before a long PCT day. As with everything on this stretch of SR 20, access is governed by the winter closure — the highway shuts in late November or early December and normally reopens between mid April and early May, though a bad winter can push it very much later, so confirm before driving. Note also that this specific trailhead has been closed at times for roadwork in recent seasons, which strands the entire zone when it happens.

sites.name: Cutthroat Pass, PCT crest camps
sites.capacity: No established or numbered sites, but a scatter of well-used flat patches on the shoulders and in the larch benches either side of the pass. Several parties can spread out. It is one of the most popular overnight spots on this stretch of trail in larch season, so a Friday arrival in late September will not have it to itself.
sites.water: NONE AT THE PASS, and this is the planning problem of the whole approach. The last certain water is on the climb up, roughly three miles from the trailhead, and there is little to nothing again until close to the lakes far ahead. Carry enough for the evening, the night and the next morning's walk, which for two people is more than most parties expect to shoulder.
sites.permit: None. Dispersed camping on national forest land needs no permit and no reservation. Camp on durable ground rather than in the meadow, and note that the quarter-mile camping closure around Cutthroat Lake, well below and to the east, does not reach up here. Forest-wide campfire bans are normal from mid summer; there is nothing worth burning at this elevation anyway.
sites.notes: Cutthroat Pass is about five miles north of Rainy Pass by a steadily graded trail and is the first natural stop for anyone heading for Golden Horn or Tower Mountain, though a fit party carrying enough water will push straight past it toward Granite Pass or the lakes. It is not a climbers' camp for any peak in this file — nothing is climbed directly from it — but it is the obvious bad-weather or late-start stop, and it is where a party discovers whether it brought enough water. The larch stands here are the reason the pass is crowded from the third week of September. This is also the point where the Cutthroat Creek trail comes up from the east, so a party can leave one car at each trailhead and walk through.

sites.name: Granite Pass
sites.capacity: One small site at the pass, room for a party or two at most. It is a stopgap rather than a destination and will not absorb a group.
sites.water: Seasonal at best. There is nothing dependable at the pass and the trail either side of it is dry. Treat this as a dry camp and plan accordingly.
sites.permit: None. National forest, dispersed camping, no permit and no quota. Northwest Forest Pass to park back at Rainy Pass.
sites.notes: Granite Pass sits a couple of miles beyond Cutthroat Pass as the trail swings north-west and begins the long traverse under Tower Mountain. Its value is position rather than comfort: it breaks the walk from Rainy Pass to Snowy Lakes into two manageable halves and it puts a party on the right side of the exposed traverse ahead. That traverse is the reason to think about timing — beyond Granite Pass the trail is cut and blasted into the cliffs, and while it is a walk in dry conditions, it is genuinely dangerous under snow. Snowfields cross the trail here into August in a normal year and an axe belongs in the pack until they have gone. Most parties passing through are heading for the lakes and stop here only when the day has run out.

sites.name: Snowy Lakes basin
sites.capacity: A number of established sites at and between the two lakes, mostly one or two tents each, plus more on the meadow benches along the PCT below the turn-off. Popular enough that a summer weekend will see several parties, and heavily so once the larches turn.
sites.water: Both lakes, and they are reliable all season. After the dry crest behind you this is where the water problem ends, which is why parties push through to it rather than stopping short.
sites.permit: None. This is national forest — no backcountry permit, no quota, nothing to book. Use the established sites rather than making new ones; the meadow here is thin, slow-growing and visibly worn where people have spread out. Campfires are a bad idea on principle at this elevation and are usually banned outright by mid summer under a forest-wide order.
sites.notes: This is THE climbers' camp for both Golden Horn and Tower Mountain and the whole point of walking the PCT north. From Rainy Pass it is roughly twenty miles round trip over Cutthroat and Granite Passes, with the trail contouring past Tower Mountain and dropping to about six thousand three hundred feet before a signed spur climbs half a mile of well-graded switchbacks to the lakes. Lower Snowy Lake comes first, Upper is a short way above. From camp, Golden Horn is taken by gullies on its south side, mostly loose class 3 scrambling, ending at a summit block where the last twenty feet of mantling above a big ledge is the one move that stops parties; Tower Mountain's west and south sides are a choice of class 3 gully systems on generally sound rock buried under loose surface debris, while its east face is a sheer wall and no business of a scrambling party. Both can be done from this camp in one long day. August and September are the season; snow on the traverse and the north-facing slopes governs anything earlier.

sites.name: Methow Pass and the PCT meadow camps below Snowy Lakes
sites.capacity: A string of established sites in the meadows along the trail around a mile beyond Methow Pass, near where the boot path to the lakes leaves. Enough ground for several parties spread out, and lower and more sheltered than the lake basin.
sites.water: Good here — this is the drainage side of the crest and the creeks running off toward the West Fork Methow are dependable. It is the reason to choose these camps over the lakes when the wind is up.
sites.permit: None. National forest, dispersed camping at established sites, no permit and no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Rainy Pass.
sites.notes: Methow Pass is where the PCT crosses from the Granite Creek side into the head of the West Fork Methow, and the camps just beyond it are the sheltered alternative to Snowy Lakes for anyone who does not want a night in the open at six thousand seven hundred feet. They cost a little climbing back up on summit morning and are worth it in bad weather. This is also the departure point for Mount Hardy by the long approach: the PCT is left near the pass and a climbers' path leads up toward the peak, which stands directly to the west. Parties combining Hardy with Golden Horn and Tower usually base here or at the lakes and take Hardy on the way out, since the ridge rambling between the lakes and Hardy's south side connects the whole group. Camping on the established sites rather than in fresh meadow matters here more than most places, because the ground is soft and the trail is walked by a steady stream of long-distance hikers all summer.

sites.name: Swamp Creek highway pullout, for Mount Hardy's south face
sites.capacity: A widened shoulder on SR 20 a couple of miles west of Rainy Pass, just east of Swamp Creek. Room for a few cars. This is a roadside start, not a camp — there are no facilities of any kind.
sites.water: Swamp Creek itself, immediately below the road, and further water on the lower slopes. None higher on the south face.
sites.permit: None to stop here. The land is national forest and no camping permit applies. Whether an overnight in a highway pullout is welcome varies, so the uncontroversial answer is to sleep at one of the developed campgrounds east of Washington Pass and drive over in the morning, or to sleep in the Rainy Pass lot.
sites.notes: This is the short way up Mount Hardy and the reason most parties never carry a pack up the PCT for it at all: about four and a half miles and four thousand one hundred feet, done comfortably in a day. Walk west along the highway across Swamp Creek, leave the road and climb north and north-east through timber to gain the prominent ridge on the south side of the peak, then follow the south face, which is largely a walk with occasional easy scrambling on loose talus. It is a different trip entirely from the PCT approach and needs no camp, so it is included here as the honest alternative rather than as a site anyone would choose to sleep at. Parties wanting Hardy together with Golden Horn and Tower should use the PCT and the Snowy Lakes or Methow Pass camps instead; parties wanting Hardy alone should start here.
